newsitem.title: UK: WORLD BONDS - Germany's rock-bottom yields to rise.
newsitem.headline: WORLD BONDS - Germany's rock-bottom yields to rise.

text.p: German bond yields are about as low as they can go and while they are not about to rocket higher any time soon, the risk is for a gradual pick-up, analysts said onMonday.
Key economic data out this week were unlikely to be the catalyst for the trek up but investors would find better prospects in buoyant U.S. Treasuries short-term, analysts said.
"We're not looking for anymore downward potential on German yields," said Michael Lewis, senior economist at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell in London.
"All the factors suggest yields should be going back above six percent over the next three months," he said.

Ten-year German bonds were yielding 5.830 percent at 1200 GMT, around late January lows for the year. Bond yields have dwindled and prices risen as the German economy trudged along at a lethargic pace with few, if any, signs of inflation to eat into returns.

Analysts said data out later in the week might rattle the market on first reading, but were unlikely to herald a miraculous recovery in the German economy. First on the list is German M3 money supply for October.

Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing sounded the warning for a potentially large figure last Friday when he said the privatisation of Deutsche Telecom -- Europe's largest share flotation ever -- could swell the data.

Holger Farinkrug, senior economist at UBS in Frankfurt, said he ratcheted up his forecast for M3 to 8.8 percent from 7.9 after Issing's comments but with a rise well-flagged and largely accounted for, the market should be able to swallow the increase. In September, M3 showed an 8.4 percent rise.
The Ifo index of business sentiment is next on the list at 0900 GMT on Wednesday.

Lewis at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell expected a rise to 96.0 from 95.7 in October with initial government data overestimating economic weakness in September. Others saw it stagnating around current levels.
Farinkrug said, "We know new orders and output were weak in September, we know unemployment was rising strongly in October. The dollar has been declining in the second half of October."
Farinkrug said recent tax discussions were not favourable for companies, further putting a dampner on corporate expectations and sentiment.
"For all these reasons I would be surprised if it went up further," he said.
While Farinkrug said there was no immediate upward pressure on Bund yields it would be difficult for the market to cling to levels below six percent.
"I don't see much immediate pressure but generally history has taught us levels below six percent are very hard to sustain in Germany," he said.
While yield convergence has been helping other markets in Europe, for Germany it could have a bearish fallout, analysts said.

The market currently had attached no risk premium to Bunds of European Economic and Monetary Union beginning on time with Italy and Spain in the starting block. But the convergence of Italian and Spanish yields on German debt should begin to take its toll on Bund yields.

Huw Roberts, European bond strategist at NatWest Capital Markets here, thinks German yields can still drop a little further with interest rates set to remain at rock bottom for some time to come, but he still favours the U.S. market.
"There is very bullish sentiment in the U.S. and Treasuries seem to want to go higher and will continue to do so at the expense of spread narrowing," he said.
"So although I think Germany can resume outperforming at some stage it's probably not the best trade to put on at the moment."
The 10-year T-note/Bund spread was at 45 basis points.
